build_inputs.angles:
1. Lead on this: this is the AP2, the one that gave up the scream for torque. Honda dropped the 2.0 for a 2.2, added mid-range, and cut about a thousand rpm off the redline - and twenty years on, owners still argue about whether that fixed the car or ruined the point of it. The 2.0 revved to 9,000. This one does not.
2. Cover the record, because it is why anyone cares. The earlier 2.0 made more horsepower per litre than any naturally aspirated production engine in the world - more power-dense than the Ferrari and Lamborghini V12s of its day, from a Honda four-cylinder - and it held that for about a decade until a Ferrari took it back. Then Honda stopped. There has never been another S2000.
3. For the head-to-head use the 2006 Porsche Boxster S - same money when new, the sensible choice, 3.4 litres and a redline about a thousand rpm below this car's. The Honda is down on power and revs past where the Porsche stops.

scenes.headline: Less Scream
scenes.narration: For 2004, Honda stretched the 2.0 to 2.2 litres for stronger midrange and dropped fuel cutoff from 9,000 to 8,200 rpm.

scenes.headline: 237 HP
scenes.narration: This naturally aspirated four makes 237 horsepower and 162 pound-feet of torque; Honda lengthened the stroke rather than widening the cylinders.

scenes.headline: World Record
scenes.narration: The original 2.0 set the world record for horsepower per litre among naturally aspirated production engines in 1999; the Ferrari 458 Italia beat it about a decade later.

scenes.headline: Torsen LSD
scenes.narration: A six-speed manual sends power rearward through a Torsen limited-slip differential without clutch packs, and Honda shortened the first five gears but made sixth taller.

scenes.headline: $34K → $43K
scenes.narration: They started at about $34,000 new, and they go for about $43,000 today.
So would you take this car's extra midrange, or sacrifice it to get that original 9,000 rpm scream back?

script: That 9,000 rpm scream's been traded for torque, and owners still argue whether that ruined the point. For 2004, Honda stretched the 2.0 to 2.2 litres for stronger midrange and dropped fuel cutoff from 9,000 to 8,200 rpm. This naturally aspirated four makes 237 horsepower and 162 pound-feet of torque; Honda lengthened the stroke rather than widening the cylinders. The original 2.0 set the world record for horsepower per litre among naturally aspirated production engines in 1999; the Ferrari 458 Italia beat it about a decade later. A six-speed manual sends power rearward through a Torsen limited-slip differential without clutch packs, and Honda shortened the first five gears but made sixth taller. They started at about $34,000 new, and they go for about $43,000 today. So would you take this car's extra midrange, or sacrifice it to get that original 9,000 rpm scream back?

sections.Highlights: THIS... is a 2006 Honda S2000, finished in Laguna Blue Pearl with a black soft top and a black interior. The odometer on this S2000 currently indicates approximately 15,700 miles. The attached Carfax vehicle history report lists no accidents or mileage discrepancies in this Honda's past. It also confirms California registration from new. Photos of VIN stickers are available in the gallery, and indicate that the body panels of this S2000 are numbers-matching. A partial list of notable equipment reported by the seller includes a limited-slip differential, a power-operated soft top, leather upholstery, a digital instrument cluster, push-button start, and air conditioning. A list of notable modifications reported by the seller is detailed below. Highlights include Air Lift Performance suspension, 17-inch Advan Racing wheels, a Rotora big brake kit, an Injen engine air intake, carbon fiber exterior components, and an aftermarket shift knob. The Honda S2000 was introduced in 1999 to celebrate Honda's 50th anniversary and quickly gained favor for its high-revving engine and balanced handling. The 2004 model year marked the introduction of significant updates, including revised suspension tuning, updated styling, and, for North America, a new 2.2-liter engine with added torque; though max revs were down by 800, the so-called F22C still spun all the way to a spine-tingling 8,200 rpm. Power comes from an F22C 2.2-liter inline-4, rated at 237 horsepower and 162 lb-ft of torque. Output is sent to the rear wheels via a 6-speed manual transmission.
